description: How social divisions shape life chances, power and social mobility — and the limits of meritocracy.
content_html:
What Are Life Chances?

Life chances is a concept associated with Max Weber. It refers to the probability that a person will enjoy the positive outcomes that a society has to offer — good health, educational success, secure employment, satisfactory housing and a long life expectancy. Weber argued that class position shapes life chances because it determines a person’s position in the market. In the UK, however, life chances are not determined by class alone. Research consistently shows that gender, race and ethnicity, sexuality, age, disability, and religion and belief all shape what individuals can realistically expect from life, often in combination.

Key Fact

The specification identifies seven factors affecting life chances: social class, gender, race and ethnicity, sexuality, age, disability and religion and belief. Each can independently and in combination with others shape a person’s access to education, employment, health and other valued resources. A person’s life chances are shaped not just by who they are but by where they are positioned in the social structure.

Social Class and Life Chances

Social class remains one of the strongest predictors of life outcomes in the UK. Children from professional and managerial backgrounds are significantly more likely to attend higher-performing schools, obtain higher-education qualifications and enter well-paid occupations than those from working-class backgrounds. They tend to have better health outcomes and longer life expectancy. This is partly explained by material deprivation — working-class families have fewer financial resources to invest in education, private healthcare or extracurricular activities. It is also explained by cultural and social capital: the values, knowledge and social networks that enable middle-class families to navigate educational and employment systems more effectively.

Private schooling is one of the most visible mechanisms of class-based advantage. Privately educated individuals are over-represented in the senior professions, the judiciary and elected politics. The informal network of contacts, shared school ties and mutual recognition among privately educated elites — sometimes described as the “old boys’ network” — represents a form of social closure that maintains class advantage across generations.

Devine and the Affluent Worker: Class Identity and Mobility

Fiona Devine’s study Affluent Workers Revisited (1992) examined how class shapes life chances and aspirations by revisiting the site of an earlier study. In the 1960s, Goldthorpe and Lockwood studied male manual workers at the Vauxhall car plant in Luton, arguing that affluent workers were becoming embourgeoisified — absorbed into middle-class values as wages rose. They proposed the concept of privatised instrumentalism — social relationships focused inward on the family.

Devine revisited Luton in the late 1980s, interviewing manual workers and their partners. She did not find evidence of full embourgeoisement: workers had not absorbed middle-class values or abandoned working-class identity. Crucially, Devine found that her respondents retained a strong sense of class identity and resentment at extreme inequality, even though many aspired to consumer goods and rising living standards. Many had also lost faith in the Labour Party to deliver greater equality. Devine’s study is significant for the life chances debate because it demonstrates that social mobility — upward movement in the class structure — does not automatically dissolve class identity or awareness of inequality. Rising wages may improve individuals’ material conditions without fundamentally changing the structure of class inequality.

Social mobility is the ability to change one’s position in the class hierarchy. Intergenerational mobility describes movement across generations — a working-class child reaching a professional occupation represents upward intergenerational mobility. Intragenerational mobility describes movement within a single lifetime — a person who starts in a manual role and rises to management through training and promotion. Functionalists see upward social mobility as evidence that the system is working meritocratically: talent is recognised and rewarded. Marxists argue that structural barriers mean mobility is limited and class position is substantially reproduced across generations — the system appears open but the evidence suggests inherited advantage is a powerful predictor of outcomes.

Gender: Women in the UK continue to earn less on average than men — the gender pay gap persists across most sectors. Women are over-represented in part-time and lower-paid work. Life expectancy is longer for women, but women are more likely to experience poverty in old age due to lower pension accumulation from career breaks.

Race and ethnicity: Ethnic minority groups face, on average, higher unemployment rates, lower wages and over-representation in lower-status occupations compared with White British groups. Institutional racism in employment and education contributes to these patterns. Sociologists are careful to distinguish between different ethnic groups and to explain ethnic inequalities using social mechanisms rather than treating ethnicity as inherently predictive.

Age: Life chances vary across the life course. Young people face higher unemployment and are less likely to own their own homes. Older workers may face ageism in the labour market, limiting promotion and earnings prospects in later working life. Elderly people on fixed incomes are more vulnerable to poverty.

Disability: Disabled people have significantly lower employment rates and, on average, lower incomes than non-disabled people. The social model of disability, as discussed in Lesson 4, argues that these inequalities are produced by social barriers rather than by impairment alone — the disability employment gap reflects both employer attitudes and inaccessible workplaces.

Sexuality: LGBTQ+ individuals face higher rates of mental health difficulties, discrimination in employment and housing, and social exclusion in some contexts. Legal protections have increased significantly since the 1960s, but inequalities in life chances persist due to ongoing discrimination and the effects of heteronormativity.

Religion and belief: Religious identity can affect life chances through employment discrimination (Islamophobia documented in hiring studies), social capital (religious communities can provide supportive networks) and cultural expectations. Some religious groups face higher rates of poverty linked to discrimination in the labour market.

Perspectives on Life Chances: Functionalist, Marxist and Feminist

Functionalists, following Davis and Moore, would argue that differential life chances reflect differential rewards for positions of varying functional importance. If some people have better life chances, this is partly because they have worked harder or demonstrated greater talent — consistent with a meritocratic system. Social mobility is evidence the system is working. Marxists argue that life chances are shaped fundamentally by class position and by the structural reproduction of inequality across generations. Material deprivation, restricted access to education and ruling class ideology ensure that class inequality in life chances is reproduced. The system is not meritocratic but serves the interests of the bourgeoisie. Feminist sociologists argue that patriarchy creates systematic inequalities in life chances for women across all class positions — even women in professional occupations face the gender pay gap and under-representation in senior roles, demonstrating that class privilege alone does not protect women from patriarchal disadvantage.

Key Fact

Devine’s 1992 study found that affluent workers had NOT become embourgeoisified: they retained class identities and resentment at extreme inequality, even as many aspired to higher living standards. This challenges the meritocratic narrative by showing that class awareness and sense of structural injustice persist even when wages rise.
exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark Describe question on factors affecting life chances, avoid listing all seven factors without developing any. The mark scheme rewards depth, not breadth. Choose two factors and describe how each affects life chances using sociological vocabulary: material deprivation, glass ceiling, ageism, institutional racism. On a 12-mark Evaluate about whether life chances are determined primarily by class, structure your answer around the Marxist view (class as fundamental, material deprivation, structural reproduction), the functionalist view (meritocratic rewards, Davis and Moore), and the feminist view (patriarchy independently shapes women’s life chances). Name Devine’s study as evidence that class identity and awareness of inequality persist even among relatively well-paid workers.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Life chances — the probability of enjoying positive outcomes such as education, health and employment — are shaped by seven factors: class, gender, race and ethnicity, sexuality, age, disability, and religion and belief, often operating in combination through material deprivation, discrimination and structural barriers.
  • Devine's 1992 study revisiting Luton found that affluent workers had not become embourgeoisified: they retained class identities and resentment at inequality, challenging privatised instrumentalism and demonstrating that rising wages do not dissolve class identity or structural awareness.
  • Functionalists see differential life chances as meritocratic; Marxists argue they reflect structural class reproduction; feminists argue patriarchy independently shapes women's life chances; all perspectives agree that social mobility exists but disagree about how much, and whose interests it serves.

practice_questions.text:
Which sociologist revisited the Luton car-plant workers in the early 1990s to study class identity and life chances?
A) Goldthorpe
B) Townsend
C) Walby
D) Devine

practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that life chances refer to the opportunities available to an individual to improve their quality of life; 1 mark for linking this to social position or structural factors. Example: 'Life chances are the opportunities an individual has to improve their quality of life, such as access to education, health and employment, which are shaped by their position in the social structure including their class, gender and ethnicity.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one way that gender affects life chances in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying one way gender affects life chances (e.g. the gender pay gap; over-representation of women in low-paid part-time work; the glass ceiling; women's greater likelihood of poverty in old age). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'Women in the UK earn less on average than men in comparable occupations, a pattern described as the gender pay gap. This affects their overall financial security, pension accumulation and economic independence over the life course. Feminist sociologists link this to patriarchal structures that undervalue women's labour and create barriers to senior positions — the glass ceiling — rather than to differences in ability or effort.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Devine's key findings from her study of affluent workers.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Devine revisited Luton in the late 1980s, interviewing manual workers and their partners at the same site as Goldthorpe and Lockwood's original 1960s study (1 mark). She did not find evidence to support embourgeoisement — workers had not absorbed middle-class values or abandoned class identity (1 mark). Workers retained a strong sense of class identity and resentment at extreme inequality despite rising living standards and consumer aspirations (1 mark). Many had also lost faith in the Labour Party as a vehicle for change, but had not abandoned their awareness of structural inequality (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that social mobility means inequality in life chances is decreasing in modern Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: at least two perspectives developed in detail, both sides, sustained vocabulary, supported judgement. Supporting the view: evidence of upward social mobility; educational expansion means more working-class students reaching university; functionalist view that meritocracy is operating. Contrasting: Marxist view that structural barriers mean mobility is limited and class inequality in life chances is reproduced across generations; Devine's finding that class identity persists even among affluent workers; private schooling and social closure as mechanisms reproducing elite advantage; evidence of persistent gender pay gap, disability employment gap, ethnic inequality. Named sociologists and precise vocabulary throughout. Supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement offered.

Developing: Mostly one-sided; some vocabulary; assertive conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description; few named sociologists; little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that social class is the most important factor shaping life chances in contemporary Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: full range of relevant arguments. Class as a factor argued in depth: material deprivation, private schooling and social closure, cultural capital, Devine's evidence that class identity and awareness of inequality persist; Marxist structural reproduction. At least two other factors developed as serious alternatives: gender (feminist perspective, Walby on patriarchy, glass ceiling, gender pay gap — affects women across all class positions); ethnicity (institutional racism, employment discrimination, structural inequality beyond individual prejudice). Functionalist counter-argument acknowledged: differential life chances may reflect meritocratic rewards for different levels of talent and effort. Evidence weighed: class remains a strong predictor but intersects with other factors. Supported judgement about whether class is the most important single factor or whether intersecting dimensions offer a more complete account.

Secure: Most arguments present; multiple factors developed; judgement offered.

Developing: Class discussed but limited treatment of other factors; weak evaluation; assertive conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description of class inequality; few named theorists; little evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: What concept did Goldthorpe and Lockwood use to describe a working-class lifestyle centred on the home, with work valued only as a means to earn money?
Devine's 1992 study found that affluent Luton workers had NOT become embourgeoisified. Which of the following best summarises her key finding?
options: Workers had fully adopted middle-class values and abandoned class identity
Workers retained class identities and resentment at extreme inequality
Workers had lost interest in trade unions and collective action
Workers aspired to move to professional occupations in the next generation

knowledge_checks.q: The ability to move up or down the social hierarchy, either across generations or within one's own lifetime, is called social _____.
Social mobility occurring between generations — for example a working-class child entering a professional occupation — is called _____ mobility.
Match each factor to the key life chances issue it creates:
right: Gender pay gap and over-representation in low-paid part-time work, limiting financial security
Ageism in the labour market and poverty risk on fixed pensions in old age
Significant employment gap and lower average incomes, linked to social barriers and employer discrimination

flashcard_questions.a: The opportunities to improve quality of life — education, health, employment, housing — shaped by social position.

flashcard_questions.q: Which sociologist first used the concept of life chances in relation to class position?

flashcard_questions.a: The theory that affluent workers adopt middle-class values and lifestyles as their wages rise, dissolving working-class identity.
A working-class lifestyle centred on home and family, with work valued only as a means to earn wages.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Devine find when she revisited the Luton car workers in the early 1990s?
flashcard_questions.a: Workers retained class identities and resentment at extreme inequality; embourgeoisement had not occurred.
Movement between class positions across generations, such as a working-class child entering a professional occupation.
Movement between class positions within a single person's own lifetime.
A lack of the material resources — income, housing, services — needed to participate fully in society.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the old boys' network operate as social closure?
flashcard_questions.a: Privately educated elites maintain access to top positions through informal networks and shared contacts, excluding those without those connections.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the Marxist perspective explain differential life chances?
flashcard_questions.a: Class position, determined by ownership of the means of production, shapes access to resources and reproduces inequality across generations.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Devine's study important for the life chances debate?
flashcard_questions.a: It shows that class identity and structural awareness persist even when wages rise, challenging the meritocratic narrative.

flashcard_questions.q: How do feminists explain gender inequality in life chances?
flashcard_questions.a: Patriarchy independently shapes women's life chances across all class positions — the glass ceiling and gender pay gap persist regardless of class.

glossary_terms.definition: The opportunities an individual has to improve their quality of life, including access to education, health, income and housing, shaped by their social position.
The ability to move up or down the social hierarchy, either across generations (intergenerational) or within a single lifetime (intragenerational).
Social mobility that occurs between generations, such as a child achieving a higher class position than their parents.
Social mobility that occurs within a person's own lifetime, such as moving from a manual job to a managerial role.
A lack of the material resources needed to participate fully in society, including income, housing and access to services.
The process by which the working class is said to adopt the attitudes, values and lifestyle of the middle class as their incomes rise.
A working-class lifestyle centred on home and family, with work valued only as a means to earn wages rather than as a source of community or identity.
The process by which certain groups restrict access to privileges or resources to their own members, excluding outsiders.
